pos: n. (the Thuringian Cistercian abbey of 1131, the first of the order in Thuringia, dissolved 1540)
etymology: German Volkenroda, the people's clearing, from Rodung, land cleared of forest.
biblical_def: Volkenroda in Thuringia was founded in 1131 and was the first Cistercian house in that land, a daughter of Kamp on the lower Rhine. Its name records what the white monks actually did: Rodung is forest cleared for the plough, and the abbey was planted in woodland that the brethren felled, drained and sowed. The Cistercian charter bound the choir monks to manual work and not to the collection of rents alone, and for four centuries Volkenroda kept granges, fishponds and a smithy worked by lay brothers. The house was dissolved in 1540 when Thuringia turned to the Reformation; the nave was pulled down, the eastern parts were kept as a parish church, and in 2001 the Christ Pavilion from the Hanover world exposition was re-erected beside the surviving fabric. The dictionary records Volkenroda chiefly for its doctrine of work. Scripture does not treat labour as a penance to be endured for merit but as the ordinary appointment of fallen man, “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19), and the apostolic rule in a Christian community is plain: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10). What the Cistercians got right was the dignity of the hands; what they got wrong was the ledger they kept it in. The believer's warrant is “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord” (Col 3:23), and his prayer over the finished field is “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines labour as exertion of body or mind; a grange as a farm with its buildings; assart as forest land cleared for tillage; a smithy as a workshop of a smith; and husbandry as the business of a farmer.
webster_full: LABOUR, n. Exertion of muscular strength or bodily powers; toil; work done, or to be done.
GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, &c.; a farm-house with the barns and other buildings.
ASSART, n. In old laws, the offense of grubbing up or cutting down forest trees; forest land cleared for tillage.
SMITHY, n. The shop of a smith; a place where smith's work is done.
HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground.
scriptures: Gen 3:19
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
corruption_summary: Thuringia's first Cistercian house, 1131, a forest clearing turned into granges and fishponds, dissolved 1540.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that labour is an appointment, not a payment. Volkenroda's lay brothers felled timber and dug ponds under a rule that reckoned the work toward merit, and the sentence that undoes the reckoning is “for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 3:19), which makes the plough a creature's duty rather than a creditor's claim.

The live temptation is the opposite error, to despise manual work because it earns nothing before God. Paul will not have it, and commanded a congregation that “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10); the motive he supplies is not merit but the Lord himself, “as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23), and the blessing sought is upon work already done and not upon work offered in trade, “the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17).

pos: n. (the Lower Saxon Cistercian abbey of 1135 which survived the Reformation as a Lutheran abbey and still has an abbot)
etymology: German Amelungsborn, Amelung's spring, from a personal name and Born, a well.
biblical_def: Amelungsborn in the Weser hills was founded in 1135 as a daughter of Altenkamp and became one of the wealthiest Cistercian houses of Lower Saxony, with granges, mills and a famous scriptorium. Its distinction is what happened next. When the duchy of Brunswick turned Lutheran the abbey was not suppressed but reformed: the community accepted the Augsburg Confession, the abbot remained an abbot, and the house continued as an evangelical foundation with a school attached. There has been an unbroken line of abbots since, and Amelungsborn is today a Lutheran abbey with a convent of preachers, the second-oldest such continuing foundation in Germany. The dictionary records it as the clearest German case of reformation rather than demolition. The Reformers did not ask for new institutions where old ones could be cleansed; they asked for the old road, “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), and the prophetic summons behind that is a return and not an invention, “Return unto me, and I will return unto you” (Mal 3:7). What was removed at Amelungsborn was the mass, the merit and the vow; what was kept was the fabric, the school and the hours of prayer. That is the pattern Christ himself prescribes for a fallen church, “repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5), and the promise to such a work is “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach” (Isa 58:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abbot as the superior of an abbey; to reform as to restore to a good state; a convent as a body of monks or nuns; a scriptorium is a writing-room; and a foundation as that on which a thing is founded, also an endowment.
webster_full: ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
REFORM, v.t. To change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state.
CONVENT, n. An assembly of religious persons; a body of monks or nuns; also, the house they occupy.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of an institution.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that on which anything stands; also, an endowment.
scriptures: Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Mal 3:7

Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. But ye said, Wherein shall we return?
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
corruption_summary: Lower Saxon Cistercian abbey of 1135, reformed rather than dissolved, a Lutheran abbey with an unbroken line of abbots.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reformation is restoration and not novelty. Amelungsborn kept its walls and lost its mass, and the prophet's own word for that order of business is “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths” (Jer 6:16), a command to look backward before building forward.

The live temptation is to read every continuity as compromise and every demolition as courage. Scripture judges otherwise: the call is “Return unto me, and I will return unto you” (Mal 3:7), the required act is “do the first works” (Rev 2:5), and the name given to those who rebuild on old ground is honourable, “The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isa 58:12).

pos: n. (the Saxon Cistercian abbey of 1137, from 1543 the princely school Schulpforta)
etymology: Latin Porta, a gate, in the abbey's style Sancta Maria ad Portam; German Pforte, a gate.
biblical_def: Pforta on the Saale, founded in 1137 and styled Sancta Maria ad Portam, was among the great Cistercian houses of Saxony, with a church of some two hundred feet and a library to match. In 1543 Duke Maurice of Saxony dissolved the community and converted the whole establishment into a Landesschule, one of three princely schools endowed out of monastic property to train ministers and magistrates for an evangelical territory. Under the name Schulpforta it became the most famous boarding school in Germany, and its roll includes Klopstock, Fichte, Leopold von Ranke and Friedrich Nietzsche. The dictionary records Pforta as the best use a dissolved abbey was ever put to in Saxony, and as a warning. Monastic endowments diverted to schools taught Greek and Hebrew to generations of pastors, and the apostolic charge for such a place is “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15), with the Berean habit as its timetable, “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). The reason for the languages is the claim made for the text, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). The warning is that a school founded to hand on the faith can keep the buildings and lose the deposit, which is why the psalmist makes transmission a duty and not a result, “shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a school as a place of instruction; a gymnasium as a place for literary exercises; a preceptor as a teacher; a gate as a large door or entrance; and tradition as delivery, the handing down of accounts.
webster_full: SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
GYMNASIUM, n. In Germany, a school of the higher order, in which the languages and sciences are taught.
PRECEPTOR, n. A teacher; an instructor; the principal of a school.
GATE, n. A large door which gives entrance into a walled city, a castle, a temple, or other inclosed place.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, by oral communication.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
corruption_summary: Saxon Cistercian abbey of 1137 turned in 1543 into Schulpforta, the princely school of Klopstock, Fichte, Ranke and Nietzsche.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an endowment spent on teaching the Scriptures is an endowment well spent. Pforta's cloister became a schoolroom where boys construed Greek, and the charge over such a room is “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15), a phrase about cutting a text straight.

The live temptation is to measure such a school by its famous names. Pforta taught Nietzsche, who left it to spend his life against the faith it was endowed to serve, and that outcome is the standing argument for making transmission deliberate: the Bereans were commended because they “received the word with all readiness of mind” (Act 17:11), the text is honoured because “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), and the duty is laid on fathers in terms that admit no delegation, “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4).

pos: n. (the Thuringian imperial free city, an early adherent of the Reformation, with a Cistercian nunnery and a royal collegiate church)
etymology: German Nordhausen, the north houses, from Nord and Haus.
biblical_def: Nordhausen at the southern foot of the Harz was a free city of the Empire from 1220, answerable to no prince but the emperor, and it held that standing for nearly six hundred years. It carried a royal collegiate church, a Cistercian nunnery and a Dominican house, and it went over to the Reformation early: the council called an evangelical preacher in 1522 and the city was formally Lutheran by 1524, among the first free cities to be so. Its civic independence is the reason. A free city could reform without waiting for a prince, and a great many of the earliest German reformations were urban for exactly that cause. The dictionary records Nordhausen as a study in lawful authority. Scripture does not treat the magistrate as an obstacle to be got round but as an ordinance to be honoured, “there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1), and it lays on citizens a positive duty toward the town they live in, “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives” (Jer 29:7). A city reformed in doctrine was expected to show it in its order, since “the work of righteousness shall be peace” (Isa 32:17), and the condition God attaches to the healing of a land is humiliation and prayer and not civic self-congratulation, “shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face” (2Ch 7:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a city as a large town with a corporation; a magistrate as a public civil officer; a franchise as a particular privilege or right; a council as an assembly for consultation; and a commonwealth as the whole body of people in a state.
webster_full: CITY, n. In a general sense, a large town; a large collection of houses and inhabitants, incorporated.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government of some branch of it.
FRANCHISE, n. A particular privilege or right granted by a prince or sovereign to an individual, or to a number of persons.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
COMMONWEALTH, n. An established form of government, or civil polity; the whole body of people in a state.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever.

If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
corruption_summary: Thuringian imperial free city, Lutheran by 1524, whose civic liberty let it reform without a prince.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that lawful civil authority is God's ordinance and not a necessary evil. Nordhausen answered to the emperor alone and used that liberty to call an evangelical preacher, and the apostolic ground of all such order is “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1).

The live temptation is to make civic liberty the gospel rather than its occasion. Nordhausen's freedom was an opportunity, not a righteousness: the duty Scripture lays on a townsman is to “pray unto the LORD for it” (Jer 29:7), the fruit it promises a reformed order is “quietness and assurance for ever” (Isa 32:17), and the terms on which any land is healed begin with repentance and not with charters, “turn from their wicked ways” (2Ch 7:14).

pos: n. (the Thuringian residence city of Ernestine Saxony, reformed under Friedrich Myconius, seat of the Gotha Confutatio)
etymology: Old High German Gotaha, the good water, from guot and aha, a stream.
biblical_def: Gotha in Thuringia was a town of the Ernestine Saxon dukes and one of the earliest settled reformations in Germany. Friedrich Myconius, a former Franciscan who had been refused a Bible by his own order, came as preacher in 1524 and remained until his death in 1546, organising parishes, visitations and a school, and serving as one of Luther's trusted men of business. Gotha afterwards became a ducal residence with a great library and a reputation for exact Lutheran orthodoxy. The dictionary records Gotha for the ordinary machinery of reform: not a pamphlet war but a preacher who stayed twenty-two years, catechised children and visited villages. The pastoral charge such a man holds is defined by what he holds fast, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9), and by the relentlessness required of him, “be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). Where doctrine was at stake Gotha's theologians were plain rather than conciliatory, which is the apostolic instinct: the faith is a deposit to be defended, “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and the measure applied to any rival message is absolute, “preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a preacher as one who discourses publicly on religious subjects; a catechism as a form of instruction by questions and answers; a visitation as the act of a superior who inspects; orthodoxy as soundness of faith; and a residence as the place of dwelling.
webster_full: PREACHER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one who delivers a sermon.
CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; the object of visits; the act of a superior or superintending officer, who inspects.
ORTHODOXY, n. Soundness of faith; a belief in the genuine doctrines taught in the Scriptures.
RESIDENCE, n. The act of abiding or dwelling in a place for some continuance of time; the place of abode.
scriptures: Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: Ernestine Thuringian residence reformed by Friedrich Myconius from 1524, afterwards a seat of exact Lutheran orthodoxy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reform is mostly residence. Myconius preached in one town for twenty-two years, and the qualification Paul names for such a man is possession of a message he did not invent, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9).

The live temptation is to mistake plainness for harshness and so to trade the deposit for a quiet parish. Scripture forbids the trade: the preacher is to “reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2), the faith is “once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) and therefore not open to revision, and the apostle will not exempt even himself from the standard, “though we, or an angel from heaven” (Gal 1:8).

pos: n. (the Thuringian residence city of the Ernestine dukes, seat of the Weimar edition of Luther's works)
etymology: Old High German Wimares, probably the holy marsh, from wih and mari.
biblical_def: Weimar in Thuringia was a seat of the Ernestine Saxon dukes, the branch of the house that protected Luther. Luther himself preached in the castle chapel more than once, Lucas Cranach died in the town and his son's great altarpiece in the Herderkirche sets the crucified Christ, Luther and Cranach in one panel with the blood falling on the painter's head, a picture of imputation rather than of patronage. Weimar later gave its name to the Weimarer Ausgabe, the critical edition of Luther's works begun in 1883 and running past a hundred volumes, which remains the scholarly text of the Reformer. The dictionary records Weimar for the durability of written words against the men who write them. Dukes, painters and editors all died; the text they were handling did not, and Scripture says why: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). Peter applies the same contrast to every human glory, “For all flesh is as grass” (1Pe 1:24). The reason a town spends a century editing a sixteenth-century preacher is that the preacher was pointing at something that does not decay, “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17), and that opening the text to ordinary people is itself the work, “The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an edition as the publication of a book; a volume as a book or a roll; to edit as to publish, to superintend a publication; a chapel as a place of worship subordinate to a church; and an altarpiece as a painting placed over the altar.
webster_full: EDITION, n. The publication of any book before published; also, the whole number of copies published at once.
VOLUME, n. A book; a roll; primarily, a roll of writing; a book, whether complete in itself or part of a work.
EDIT, v.t. To publish; more usually, to superintend a publication; to prepare a book or paper for the public eye.
CHAPEL, n. A house for public worship; a place of worship subordinate to a parish church.
ALTAR-PIECE, n. A painting placed over the altar in a church.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
corruption_summary: Ernestine residence where Luther preached and Cranach painted, afterwards the name of the standard edition of Luther's works.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the written word outlasts its handlers. A hundred volumes of Luther were edited at Weimar by men now themselves dead, and the sentence that explains why the labour was worth it is “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).

The live temptation is to let a reformer's collected works take the place his own works assign to Scripture. Weimar's edition is a tool and not a testimony: all flesh, Luther's included, is “as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass” (1Pe 1:24); the sanctifying instrument is named exactly, “thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17); and what it is given to do is to reach the unlearned, “it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word, a thing spoken; Greek rhema (G4487), a spoken word; Greek aletheia (G0225), truth; Hebrew pethi (H6612), the simple, the untaught.

“The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — why the text must be opened, not kept.

pos: n. (the Harz Cistercian abbey of 1146, dissolved in the Reformation, now a school of early music)
etymology: German Michaelstein, Michael's stone, from the dedication and Stein, a rock.
biblical_def: Michaelstein near Blankenburg in the Harz was founded in 1146 as a Cistercian house and kept the usual Cistercian economy of granges, fishponds and a water system still partly traceable. It was dissolved in 1543 when the county turned Lutheran, served afterwards as a domain farm, and in the twentieth century became an institute and school for early music, with the cloister used for rehearsal and the refectory for concerts. The dictionary records Michaelstein for the Cistercian discipline of silence, which the order kept more strictly than most and which its buildings were designed to serve: no sculpture in the cloister, no tower on the church, signs instead of speech in the walks. Scripture grounds silence not in technique but in who is present, “let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20), and the command is to stop and know rather than to empty the mind, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10). Waiting of this kind is commended as good and not merely as useful, “It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26), and the figure given it is a watchman through a long night, “My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning” (Psa 130:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines silence as absence of sound, also forbearance of speech; a cloister as a covered walk in a monastery; a refectory as a room for meals; to meditate as to dwell on anything in thought; and plain-song as the simple unisonous melody of the church.
webster_full: SILENCE, n. In a general sense, stillness, or entire absence of sound or noise; also, forbearance of speech in man.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a covered passage or walk round a court, usually with a colonnade.
REFECTORY, n. A room of refreshment; a hall or apartment in convents, where they take their meals.
MEDITATE, v.i. To dwell on anything in thought; to contemplate; to study; to turn or revolve any subject in the mind.
PLAIN-SONG, n. The simple notes of an air unvaried by artificial graces; the unisonous chant of the church.
scriptures: Hab 2:20
But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
Lam 3:26
It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.
My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning.
corruption_summary: Harz Cistercian abbey of 1146, built for the order's discipline of silence, now a school of early music.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that biblical silence is attention and not vacancy. Michaelstein's cloister was built bare on purpose, and the ground the prophet gives for hushing a whole world is a Person and a place, “But the LORD is in his holy temple” (Hab 2:20).

The live temptation is to borrow the monastic hush as a technique for quieting the self while dropping the object it was meant to attend to. Scripture ties the stillness to a proposition: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10). The waiting it commends has an object, “quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26), and an expectation, since the watchman watches “for the morning” (Psa 130:6) and not for nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew damam (H1826), to be silent, to be still; Hebrew raphah (H7503), to be slack, to cease; Hebrew qavah (H6960), to wait, to look for; Hebrew shamar (H8104), to keep watch.
roots_lines: Hebrew hasah (H2013) — to hush, to keep silence; “let all the earth keep silence before him”, Habakkuk 2:20.
Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to be slack, to let go, to be still; “Be still, and know that I am God”, Psalm 46:10.
Hebrew yachal (H3176) — to hope, to wait; “both hope and quietly wait”, Lamentations 3:26.
Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look eagerly for; “My soul waiteth for the Lord”, Psalm 130:6.
Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, to watch, to guard; “they that watch for the morning”, Psalm 130:6.
usage: “let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20) — silence with a reason attached.
“Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10) — stillness that ends in knowledge.
“quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26) — what the waiting is actually for.

pos: n. (the Brandenburg Cistercian abbey of 1170, a colonising house whose lands became a weaving town)
etymology: Probably Slavic cyna, a boundary or marshy place, latinised as Cinna.
biblical_def: Zinna south of Berlin was founded about 1170 by the archbishop of Magdeburg and settled from Altenberg, and it belongs to the eastward Cistercian colonisation of the Flāming: marsh drained, villages laid out on a plan, German and Flemish settlers brought in under written tenancies. The abbey ran granges, a brewery and a tile works, and after its dissolution in 1553 the Prussian crown planted a weavers' colony on its lands, so that Kloster Zinna became a manufacturing village with the abbey church at its centre. The dictionary records Zinna for the plain economics of monastic life, which were the real engine of the order and the real occasion of its decay. There is nothing unspiritual in profit honestly got, “In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23), and the apostolic end of a working trade is not accumulation but relief, “that he may have to give to him that needeth” (Eph 4:28). The danger is scale. A house that begins by draining its own marsh and ends by managing estates is being tested in a particular way, since “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10), and the single requirement laid on a man who handles what is not his own is not shrewdness but fidelity, “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a grange as a farm with its buildings; a tenant as one who holds lands of another; a colony as a body of people removed to a new country; a weaver as one who weaves; and profit as gain, advantage.
webster_full: GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, &c.; a farm-house with the barns and other buildings.
TENANT, n. One who holds or possesses lands or tenements by any kind of right or title.
COLONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.
WEAVER, n. One who weaves; one whose occupation is to weave cloth.
PROFIT, n. Gain; advantage; any accession of good from labor or exertion.
scriptures: In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
Eph 4:28
Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
corruption_summary: Brandenburg Cistercian house of 1170 that drained the Flaming and planted villages; its lands became a Prussian weaving colony.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that honest gain is lawful and that its purpose is giving. Zinna drained marsh and ran a tile works, and the proverb that blesses such industry is blunt about results, “In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23).

The live temptation is the one the Cistercians actually fell into: an order founded on austerity became a landlord, and the test it failed was a test of fidelity rather than of competence. The apostolic purpose of a trade is “to give to him that needeth” (Eph 4:28); the Lord makes small sums the assay of large ones, “he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much” (Luk 16:10); and the one thing asked of a steward is stated without alternatives, “that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).
roots_summary: Hebrew mothar (H4195), profit, advantage; Greek kopiao (G2872), to toil; Greek oikonomos (G3623), a steward; Greek pistos (G4103), faithful.
roots_lines: Hebrew mothar (H4195) — profit, that which remains over; “In all labour there is profit”, Proverbs 14:23.
Greek kopiao (G2872) — to toil, to labour to weariness; “let him labour, working with his hands”, Ephesians 4:28.
Greek chreia (G5532) — need, necessity; “to him that needeth”, Ephesians 4:28.
Greek elachistos (G1646) — least, smallest; “faithful in that which is least”, Luke 16:10.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward, a house-manager; “it is required in stewards”, 1 Corinthians 4:2.
usage: “In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23) — gain is not the sin.
“that he may have to give to him that needeth” (Eph 4:28) — what the gain is for.
“that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2) — the whole of a steward's job description.

pos: n. (the Lower Saxon house of 986, a Benedictine nunnery which continued after the Reformation as a Lutheran ladies' foundation)
etymology: German Walsrode, Wal's clearing, from a personal name and Rodung, cleared land.
biblical_def: Walsrode on the Lūneburg heath was founded in 986 as a house of religious women and is among the oldest foundations in Lower Saxony. It became Benedictine, and at the Reformation it was neither suppressed nor left as it was: the community accepted the evangelical faith and continued as a Damenstift, a Lutheran foundation of unmarried gentlewomen under an abbess, with the vows gone and the common life, the charity and the hours of worship retained. It continues on that footing to this day. The dictionary records Walsrode as the test case for what the Reformation did and did not object to in the convent. It objected to the vow, because a vow once made binds absolutely, “thou shalt not slack to pay it” (Deu 23:21), and a rash perpetual vow of celibacy therefore lays a snare that Scripture refuses to lay, naming the forbidding of marriage among the marks of departing doctrine, “Forbidding to marry” (1Ti 4:3). Marriage is not a lower estate, since “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” (Heb 13:4), and the apostle supplies the remedy without embarrassment, “let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn” (1Co 7:9). What survived at Walsrode was the household of unmarried women serving the poor, which no text forbids.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abbess as the superior of a nunnery; a nunnery as a house for nuns; a vow as a solemn promise made to God; celibacy as an unmarried state; and a dowry as the portion a woman brings.
webster_full: ABBESS, n. A female superior or governess of a nunnery or convent of nuns.
NUNNERY, n. A house in which nuns reside; a cloister or place of retirement for women who devote themselves to a religious life.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity; a solemn promise.
CELIBACY, n. An unmarried state; a single life; chiefly applied to a voluntary unmarried life.
DOWRY, n. The money, goods or estate which a woman brings to her husband in marriage.
scriptures: When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee.
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.
corruption_summary: Lower Saxon women's house of 986 which became a Lutheran ladies' foundation, keeping the common life and losing the vow.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Reformation struck at the vow and not at the single life. Walsrode kept its abbess and its charity and gave up its oaths, and the reason is that Scripture treats a vow as absolutely binding once uttered, “for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee” (Deu 23:21).

The live temptation is to read any honoured celibacy as the error, or any marriage as the compromise. Both readings miss the text. Paul lists the prohibition of marriage among doctrines that depart from the faith, “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3); the estate itself is pronounced honourable without qualification, “Marriage is honourable in all” (Heb 13:4); and the counsel to those who cannot contain is given plainly, “it is better to marry than to burn” (1Co 7:9).
roots_summary: Hebrew neder (H5088), a vow; Hebrew achar (H0309), to delay; Greek koluo (G2967), to forbid, to hinder; Greek timios (G5093), honourable, held in price.
roots_lines: Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow, a thing promised to God; “When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God”, Deuteronomy 23:21.
Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, to require; “will surely require it of thee”, Deuteronomy 23:21.
Greek koluo (G2967) — to forbid, to hinder, to withhold; “Forbidding to marry”, 1 Timothy 4:3.
Greek timios (G5093) — honourable, costly, held in price; “Marriage is honourable in all”, Hebrews 13:4.
Greek puroo (G4448) — to burn, to be inflamed; “than to burn”, 1 Corinthians 7:9.
usage: “thou shalt not slack to pay it” (Deu 23:21) — why a rash vow is a snare.
“Forbidding to marry” (1Ti 4:3) — the doctrine the Reformers struck at.
“Marriage is honourable in all” (Heb 13:4) — the estate the cloister had ranked lower.

pos: n. (the Westphalian Cistercian abbey of 1140, the first of the order in Westphalia)
etymology: German Hardehausen, the houses on the wooded ridge, from Hard, a wood, and Haus.
biblical_def: Hardehausen in the Egge hills was founded in 1140 from Kamp and was the first Cistercian house in Westphalia, the mother of Marienfeld, Bredelar and other daughters. It was built on the standard plan the order carried across Europe, a plan that is itself a doctrine: the church set east, the cloister square against it, the water led under the buildings, everything repeated with so little variation that a monk could be moved a thousand miles and still find the dormitory stair. The abbey was secularised in 1803 and is now a diocesan educational house. The dictionary records Hardehausen for that habit of building on a settled plan, and for the limit of the figure. A wise builder is one who first hears and then does, “which built his house upon a rock” (Mat 7:24), and the rock in the apostolic writings is named and not left open, “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11). The foundation is laid by God and not by an order, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone” (Isa 28:16), and no amount of stonework can supply what only grace supplies, which is why the psalmist mocks the early rising of men who build without Him, “It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late” (Psa 127:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a foundation as the basis of an edifice; a corner-stone as the stone which unites two walls at the corner; a plan as a draught of a building; a mother-church as the church from which others spring; and secularize as to convert from sacred to common use.
webster_full: FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground.
CORNER-STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone.
PLAN, n. A draught or form; properly, the representation of anything drawn on a plane, as a map or chart.
MOTHER-CHURCH, n. The church from which others have sprung; a metropolitan church.
SECULARIZE, v.t. To make worldly; to convert from spiritual or ecclesiastical appropriation to secular use.
scriptures: Mat 7:24
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
corruption_summary: Westphalia's first Cistercian house, 1140, mother of Marienfeld and Bredelar, built on the order's uniform plan.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a foundation is laid, not chosen. Hardehausen repeated a plan it had received rather than inventing one, and the apostolic sentence that governs every such repetition is “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid” (1Co 3:11).

The live temptation is to treat the building itself as the obedience. Christ ties the stability of the house to hearing and doing, “Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them” (Mat 7:24); the stone is God's own placing and not the builder's, “a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation” (Isa 28:16); and the psalmist's verdict on industry without Him is directed precisely at long hours, “to eat the bread of sorrows” (Psa 127:2).
roots_summary: Greek themelios (G2310), a foundation; Greek petra (G4073), a rock, a mass of rock; Hebrew pinnah (H6438), a corner; Hebrew musad (H4143), a foundation.
roots_lines: Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation, that which is laid down; “For other foundation can no man lay”, 1 Corinthians 3:11.
Greek petra (G4073) — a rock, a mass of living rock; “which built his house upon a rock”, Matthew 7:24.
Hebrew pinnah (H6438) — a corner, a corner-stone; “a precious corner stone”, Isaiah 28:16.
Hebrew bachan (H0974) — to try, to test as metal; “a tried stone”, Isaiah 28:16.
Hebrew shaveh (H7723) — vain, empty, to no purpose; “It is vain for you to rise up early”, Psalm 127:2.
usage: “which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11) — the only foundation on offer.
“which built his house upon a rock” (Mat 7:24) — the wise builder hears first.
“It is vain for you to rise up early” (Psa 127:2) — the verdict on building without Him.
